SkillClone: Multi-Modal Clone Detection and Clone Propagation Analysis in the Agent Skill Ecosystem

Conference: The 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering; October 12–16, 2026; Munich, GermanyThe 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026), October 12–16, 2026, Munich, GermanyCCS: Software and its engineering Software maintenance toolsCCS: Software and its engineering Software libraries and repositoriesCCS: Security and privacy Software security engineering
Jiaying Zhu Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore email: jiaying007@e.ntu.edu.sg , Lyuye Zhang Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore email: zh0004ye@e.ntu.edu.sg , Wenbo Guo Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore email: honywenair@gmail.com and Yang Liu Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore, Singapore email: yangliu@ntu.edu.sg
© , 2026
Abstract.

Agent skills are modular instruction packages that combine YAML metadata, natural language instructions, and embedded code, and they have reached 196K publicly available instances, yet no mechanism exists to detect clone relationships among them. This gap creates systemic risks: a vulnerability in a widely copied skill silently persists across derivatives with no alert to maintainers. Existing clone detectors, designed for single-modality source code, cannot handle the multi-modal structure of skills, where clone evidence is distributed across three interleaved content channels. We present SkillClone, the first multi-modal clone detection approach for agent skills. SkillClone fuses flat TF-IDF similarity with per-channel decomposition (YAML, NL, code) through logistic regression, combining strong detection with interpretable type classification. We construct SkillClone-Bench, a balanced benchmark of 300 ground-truth pairs with stratified difficulty. On SkillClone-Bench, SkillClone achieves F1 of 0.939 with precision 0.952, outperforming flat TF-IDF (F1 = 0.881) and achieving 4.2×\times higher Type-4 (semantic) recall than MinHash. Applying SkillClone to 20K skills reveals 258K clone pairs involving 75% of all skills, with 40% crossing author boundaries. A deduplication analysis shows the ecosystem is inflated 3.5×\times: only 5,642 unique skill concepts underlie the 20K listed skills, and 41% of skills in clone families are superseded by a strictly better variant.

Keywords: 
agent skills, clone detection, multi-modal analysis, software ecosystem, security propagation

1. Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents have rapidly evolved from standalone chatbots into extensible platforms that delegate specialized tasks to modular instruction packages called agent skills. A skill is a structured document, typically a SKILL.md file, that bundles YAML metadata, natural language instructions, and embedded code blocks into a single artifact that an LLM agent such as Claude Code, Cursor, or Windsurf can load at runtime to acquire new capabilities. Since the public launch of skill ecosystems in late 2025, adoption has been explosive: over 196K skills are now publicly available on registries and GitHub repositories, spanning domains from code generation and security analysis to DevOps automation. This growth mirrors the early trajectories of package ecosystems like npm and PyPI (Zimmermann et al., 2019; Decan et al., 2019), which took years to reach comparable scale. Recent surveys (Xu and Yan, 2026) and empirical studies (Ling et al., 2026) have begun to characterize this ecosystem’s architecture and growth dynamics.

Despite this rapid expansion, the agent skill ecosystem lacks fundamental infrastructure that traditional package ecosystems take for granted. Skills declare no dependencies on other skills, carry no version identifiers, and provide no provenance metadata linking derived skills to their origins. When a developer copies, adapts, or extends an existing skill, this relationship is entirely invisible to the ecosystem. The consequence is a growing body of duplicated and near-duplicated content whose relationships cannot be traced, audited, or monitored. This situation creates concrete security risks: when a vulnerability is discovered in a widely copied skill, there is no mechanism to identify which other skills share its content and therefore share the same flaw. Unlike a CVE advisory that can propagate through a dependency graph in npm (Liu et al., 2022), a flawed skill pattern can silently persist across hundreds of derivative skills with no alert to their maintainers. The January 2026 ClawHavoc campaign (Koi Security, 2026), which infiltrated over 1,200 malicious skills into the OpenClaw registry, demonstrated the real-world consequences of this gap.

Existing tools for skill analysis treat each skill as an isolated unit. SkillScan (Liu et al., 2026b) performs static security checks on individual skill files. SkillFortify (Bhardwaj, 2026) validates skill structure and metadata quality. MalTool (Liu et al., 2026a) detects malicious intent in single skills through behavioral analysis. SkillJect (Jia et al., 2026) and SKILL-INJECT (Schmotz et al., 2026) have demonstrated that skills serve as potent attack vectors for prompt injection (Schmotz et al., 2025). Yet none of these tools examine relationships between skills, and no prior work has studied clone patterns at ecosystem scale, despite extensive evidence from traditional package ecosystems that such relationships are critical for security (Zimmermann et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2022). The absence of such analysis means that the community cannot answer basic questions: How prevalent is skill cloning? Do clone relationships cross organizational boundaries? What is the blast radius when a hub skill contains a vulnerability?

The key insight behind our work is that agent skills are inherently multi-modal documents that resist analysis by any single similarity technique. For the dominant SKILL.md format studied in this paper, we scope the artifact to its three primary in-file modalities: YAML metadata specifying the skill’s name, tags, and configuration; natural language prose describing when and how to apply the skill; and embedded code blocks implementing concrete functionality. This scope targets the content carried directly inside the skill file, not auxiliary repository artifacts such as images, linked documents, or external scripts. Detecting clones requires fusing similarity signals across these three channels, because two skills may share identical code blocks while differing in their natural language framing, or may paraphrase the same instructions while referencing different code examples.

Preliminary ecosystem analysis revealed that clone relationships are not rare edge cases but a dominant organizing force in the ecosystem: most skills participate in at least one clone relationship, a substantial fraction of clones cross author boundaries, and malicious patterns often propagate through these latent reuse links. These observations motivate a hybrid contribution. We study undeclared reuse empirically at ecosystem scale, and we introduce a multi-modal clone detector designed specifically for the mixed YAML, natural-language, and code structure of skills.

To address this gap, we present SkillClone, the first approach for detecting clone relationships across the agent skill ecosystem. SkillClone implements a three-channel clone detection approach that synergistically computes similarity over YAML metadata, natural language instructions, and embedded code blocks, then fuses these signals through a weighted aggregation scheme to produce a unified clone score for each skill pair. We apply SkillClone to a representative sample of 20K skills drawn from the 196K-skill corpus crawled from GitHub and construct the first ecosystem-wide clone graph, where nodes represent skills and edges represent detected clone relationships. Over this graph, we perform blast radius analysis to quantify how a vulnerability in a single skill can propagate through chains of clones.

An important distinction underlies our work: clone detection identifies structural similarity between artifacts, but does not by itself establish causal reuse (i.e., that one skill was derived from another). Establishing reuse requires additional provenance signals such as fork relationships, commit timestamps, or explicit attribution. We validate that our clone detection enables downstream reuse discovery by confirming provenance in fork-mined pairs and identifying real-world clone-and-rebrand cases (Section 2.3). For security applications, the distinction is immaterial: whether two skills share a vulnerability through copying or convergent development, the blast radius is the same.

Our analysis reveals several findings with implications for ecosystem governance. Among the 258K clone relationships detected by SkillClone, 40% cross author boundaries, indicating substantial cross-organizational cloning. A deduplication analysis shows the ecosystem is inflated 3.5×\times: only 5,642 unique skill concepts underlie the 20K listed skills, and 41% of skills in clone families are superseded by a strictly better variant. Security propagation analysis identifies 141 real security-relevant skills whose dangerous patterns (SQL injection payloads, reverse shells, XSS vectors) propagate to 1,100 clones across 119 affected authors. These findings demonstrate that per-skill security tools are insufficient and that ecosystem-level clone analysis is essential for managing systemic risk.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    An empirical characterization of undeclared reuse across 20K agent skills, revealing ecosystem-scale clone prevalence, cross-author reuse, and the dominance of Type-4 semantic clones (Section 4).

  • •

    The first multi-modal clone detection approach for agent skills, fusing YAML, natural language, and code similarity signals through cross-modal alignment to detect clone relationships in heterogeneous skill documents (Section 3).

  • •

    A blast-radius analysis over the inferred clone graph, quantifying how malicious or vulnerable skill patterns propagate through latent reuse links that per-skill scanners cannot see (Section 4).

  • •

    SkillClone-Bench, a balanced benchmark of 300 annotated skill pairs with stratified difficulty, for evaluating clone detection on multi-modal skill documents.

2. Background and Motivation

2.1. Agent Skills

An agent skill is a structured document that extends an LLM agent’s capabilities at runtime. The dominant format, SKILL.md (Xu and Yan, 2026; Ling et al., 2026), consists of three primary in-file content channels that together capture the predominant content modalities of the skill file itself. The YAML frontmatter specifies metadata: skill name, description, category tags, compatibility constraints, and configuration parameters. The natural language body provides behavioral instructions about when to activate the skill, how to interact with the user, and what constraints to observe. Embedded code blocks implement concrete functionality such as shell commands, API calls, or file manipulation routines. A single skill may contain code blocks in multiple languages (e.g., Python, Bash, JavaScript), interleaved with NL prose. Chen et al. (Xu and Yan, 2026) report that this three-part structure of YAML frontmatter, NL body, and code fences is used by over 95% of skills across major registries, making it the de facto standard. Li et al. (Ling et al., 2026) confirm that 78% of skills contain at least one code block, while virtually all contain NL instructions, establishing that our three-channel decomposition covers the predominant content modalities of SKILL.md files. We therefore treat YAML and code as optional channels that may be absent in individual skills, but still part of the dominant format at ecosystem scale. This decomposition does not attempt to model auxiliary repository context beyond the focal SKILL.md artifact, such as external assets, linked files, or project history. Skills are distributed through registries (e.g., SkillsMP) and GitHub repositories, with no package manager, versioning system, or dependency declaration mechanism.

Ecosystem Scale. In our SkillsMP registry snapshot, we observe 196,134 listed skills spanning 15 major categories including code generation, testing, DevOps, security analysis, and documentation. The ecosystem has grown 4×\times in six months, driven by the adoption of agent-based development tools. Unlike traditional package ecosystems where reuse is mediated by dependency declarations (package.json in npm, requirements.txt in PyPI), skill duplication is entirely informal: a developer who wants to build on an existing skill simply copies the SKILL.md file and modifies it. This copy-and-modify workflow creates pervasive undeclared cloning that is invisible to the ecosystem.

2.2. Clone Detection: From Code to Skills

Code clone detection classifies clone relationships into four types (Roy et al., 2009). Table 1 presents these types alongside our adapted definitions for multi-modal agent skills, which must consider similarity across three content channels (YAML, NL, Code) rather than a single source language.

A key distinction is that skill clone types are determined by the joint similarity profile across channels. Two skills may exhibit Type-2 similarity in code (variable renaming) but Type-4 in NL (completely rewritten instructions), requiring a multi-modal judgment that no single-channel detector can provide. Section 3.7 operationalizes these definitions with per-channel similarity thresholds. Our taxonomy captures structural clone evidence, not proven derivation: Type-4 is the most uncertainty-prone category and excludes pairs that are merely topically related or belong to the same skill category.

Existing detectors operate on single-modality source code. Text-based approaches such as NiCad (Roy and Cordy, 2008) normalize source lines, achieving high precision for Type-1/2 but struggling with semantic clones. Token-based approaches such as SourcererCC (Sajnani et al., 2016) and CCFinder (Kamiya et al., 2002) achieve scalability through index-based filtering but remain limited to surface-level similarity. Tree-based (Baxter et al., 1998; Jiang et al., 2007) and graph-based (Krinke, 2001) approaches compare AST or PDG representations, requiring parseable single-language input. Recent ML-based approaches (Feng et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021) leverage transformer architectures to detect semantic clones on benchmarks like BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al., 2014). All these approaches assume single-language, single-modality input, an assumption that does not hold for agent skills, which interleave three structurally different content types within a single document.

2.3. Motivating Example

Figure 1 shows a real clone pair discovered by SkillClone. The original skill (sis_{i}), a 12.6K-character IDOR vulnerability testing methodology by zebbern, contains 26 code blocks (51% code by bytes). A second author (Dokhacgiakhoa) adapted this skill into a modular format: the code blocks were extracted to 24 sub-skill files and the NL body was replaced with links. Yet the author: zebbern attribution and the trigger description were preserved verbatim—confirming derivation despite the restructuring.

This pair exhibits cross-channel asymmetry: YAML similarity is high (∼{\sim}0.95), NL is moderate (∼{\sim}0.60), and code is zero. A code-only detector like SourcererCC (Sajnani et al., 2016) sees no code overlap and misses the clone entirely. A flat-text detector conflates the similarity with same-category vocabulary overlap. Only a multi-modal approach that reasons about per-channel evidence—and treats the absence of a channel as a signal rather than noise—can reliably detect this type of adaptation. The security implication is direct: any flaw in sis_{i}’s exploitation methodology propagates through sjs_{j}’s sub-skills, invisible to code-level scanners.

3. Approach

This section presents SkillClone, our approach for detecting multi-modal clone relationships among agent skills. We first formalize the problem (Section 3.1), give an overview of the approach (Section 3.2), then detail multi-modal decomposition (Section 3.3), modality-specific encoding (Section 3.4), cross-modal fusion (Section 3.5), and clone type classification (Section 3.7).

3.1. Problem Definition

Input. A corpus of NN agent skill documents 𝒮={s1,…,sN}\mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},\ldots,s_{N}\}, where each skill sis_{i} is a structured document containing YAML metadata yiy_{i}, natural language instructions nin_{i}, and embedded code blocks ci={b1,…,bk}c_{i}=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}\}.

Output. A set of clone pairs 𝒞⊆𝒮×𝒮\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{S} where each pair (si,sj,τ,σ)∈𝒞(s_{i},s_{j},\tau,\sigma)\in\mathcal{C} is annotated with clone type τ∈{Type-1,Type-2,Type-3,Type-4}\tau\in\{\text{Type-1},\text{Type-2},\text{Type-3},\text{Type-4}\} and confidence σ∈[0,1]\sigma\in[0,1].

Goal. Maximize detection F1 for true clone relationships across all four clone types, with particular emphasis on Type-3 and Type-4 semantic clones that syntactic detectors miss.

We adapt the classical clone type taxonomy (Roy et al., 2009) to multi-modal skills: Type-1 denotes identical content across all channels after whitespace normalization; Type-2 denotes cosmetic changes such as variable renaming in code or minor metadata edits; Type-3 denotes structural modifications including added or removed instructions; and Type-4 denotes skills with the same functional intent but substantially different implementation.

3.2. Approach Overview

Figure 2 illustrates our four-phase approach. The design reflects two principles. First, modality awareness: each content channel is encoded with techniques suited to its semantics rather than treating the skill as flat text. Second, cross-channel interaction: rather than scoring channels independently and taking a weighted sum, the fusion mechanism models pairwise interactions between channel similarities, capturing patterns such as “high YAML and moderate NL but absent code” that indicate structural adaptation (as in Figure 1).

3.3. Multi-Modal Decomposition

Each skill sis_{i} is decomposed into a quadruple si=(yi,ni,ci,𝐟i)s_{i}=(y_{i},n_{i},c_{i},\mathbf{f}_{i}): the YAML metadata yiy_{i} extracted from the frontmatter (fields: name, description, category, tags); the natural language instructions nin_{i} comprising the behavioral specification after the frontmatter, with code fences removed; the code component ci={b1,…,bk}c_{i}=\{b_{1},\ldots,b_{k}\} collecting all fenced code blocks with their language annotations; and a structural feature vector 𝐟i∈ℝ8\mathbf{f}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{8} capturing document-level statistics.

The decomposition uses regex-based parsing to identify YAML frontmatter (delimited by ---), code fences (delimited by ‘‘‘), and the remaining NL body. We filter boilerplate entries by removing skills with fewer than five meaningful tokens after stopword removal.

The structural feature vector 𝐟i\mathbf{f}_{i} captures eight document-level properties: total word count, number of code blocks, code-to-text ratio, average code block length, number of unique programming languages, presence of YAML frontmatter, number of YAML fields, and description length. These features capture the shape of a skill document, because two skills with similar structure (e.g., same number of code blocks, similar code fraction) are more likely to be clones than skills with different structural profiles. Each feature is min-max normalized across the corpus.

3.4. Modality-Specific Encoding

We encode each channel using latent semantic analysis (LSA) (Deerwester et al., 1990): channel-specific TF-IDF vectorization (Manning et al., 2008) followed by truncated SVD projection to d=256d=256 dimensions, producing dense embeddings that capture semantic similarity within each modality. This design follows established practices in both NL document similarity (Deerwester et al., 1990; Manning et al., 2008) and code clone detection (Sajnani et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2009), adapting them to the multi-modal skill setting. For the NL channel, TF-IDF+LSA captures topical similarity in a manner analogous to sentence embedding approaches (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), while avoiding external API dependencies. For the code channel, our language-aware tokenization follows the token-based tradition of CCFinder (Kamiya et al., 2002) and SourcererCC (Sajnani et al., 2016), extended with cross-language normalization for the multi-language code blocks found in skills.

This approach provides three advantages over neural encoders for our setting: it requires no API calls or GPU resources, enabling full reproducibility; it naturally handles the heterogeneous vocabulary across channels (YAML key-value pairs, free-form text, multi-language code); and it scales linearly with corpus size. Neural alternatives such as CodeBERT (Feng et al., 2020), GraphCodeBERT (Guo et al., 2021), and UniXcoder (Guo et al., 2022) achieve strong results on single-language code clone benchmarks, but assume homogeneous input with a single programming language per document, which does not hold for skills interleaving Python, Bash, and YAML within the same file.

YAML Channel. We serialize the YAML metadata by concatenating key-value pairs and project through TF-IDF+SVD to produce 𝐞iy∈ℝd\mathbf{e}^{y}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, capturing taxonomic relatedness.

NL Channel. The natural language body is tokenized with standard preprocessing (lowercasing, stopword removal) and encoded through TF-IDF+SVD, producing 𝐞in∈ℝd\mathbf{e}^{n}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that captures semantic similarity between behavioral specifications in the latent space.

Code Channel. Code blocks require specialized tokenization: (1) camelCase/snake_case splitting, (2) operator token extraction preserving semantically meaningful operators (|>, =>), and (3) language tag prefixing (__lang_python__) enabling cross-language discrimination. The resulting tokens are encoded through TF-IDF+SVD to produce 𝐞ic∈ℝd\mathbf{e}^{c}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

3.5. Cross-Modal Similarity Fusion

The three per-channel embeddings and the structural features capture complementary facets of skill relatedness. Following the principle that multi-modal fusion outperforms any single modality (Liang et al., 2024; Radford et al., 2021), the core technical contribution of SkillClone is a fusion mechanism that combines per-channel similarity with learned cross-channel interaction terms, producing a calibrated clone probability rather than an ad hoc score.

The IDOR clone from Figure 1 illustrates the central fusion challenge. In that pair, sjs_{j} contains zero code blocks, yielding simc=0.00\text{sim}_{c}=0.00. A fixed weighted sum that includes this zero dilutes the strong YAML (∼0.95{\sim}0.95) and NL (∼0.60{\sim}0.60) signals, risking a false negative. More subtly, the combination of high YAML and moderate NL is stronger evidence than either signal alone: metadata identity plus partial instruction overlap indicates deliberate adaptation, not coincidence. The fusion mechanism must therefore (i) adapt to absent channels and (ii) model interactions between present channels.

Intra-channel similarity. For each candidate pair (si,sj)(s_{i},s_{j}), we compute per-channel cosine similarities within each modality’s latent space:

(1) simm​(i,j)=cos⁡(𝐞im,𝐞jm),m∈{y,n,c}\text{sim}_{m}(i,j)=\cos(\mathbf{e}^{m}_{i},\mathbf{e}^{m}_{j}),\quad m\in\{y,n,c\}

Each similarity is defined only when both skills have non-trivial content in channel mm; we formalize this below.

Similarity profile. We collect the per-channel similarities into a single vector that characterizes the pair’s multi-modal relationship:

(2) 𝐬⁡(i,j)=[simy​(i,j),simn​(i,j),simc​(i,j)]∈[0,1]3\mathbf{s}(i,j)=\bigl[\text{sim}_{y}(i,j),\;\text{sim}_{n}(i,j),\;\text{sim}_{c}(i,j)\bigr]\in[0,1]^{3}

The similarity profile is the primary representation for downstream clone detection: its geometry directly encodes clone type (Type-1 pairs cluster near (1,1,1)(1,1,1); Type-4 pairs exhibit high simn\text{sim}_{n} with low simc\text{sim}_{c}), making it a richer object than any scalar summary.

Channel presence. Not every skill contains every modality. We define a binary presence indicator per channel:

(3) Pm​(i,j)={1if channel ​m​ is non-trivially present in both ​si,sj0otherwiseP_{m}(i,j)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if channel }m\text{ is non-trivially present in both }s_{i},s_{j}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}

When Pm=0P_{m}=0, the corresponding simm\text{sim}_{m} is set to zero. Critically, a missing channel is absence of evidence, not evidence of dissimilarity. The logistic model (below) learns this distinction from training pairs that include both present and absent channels. In the IDOR example, Pc​(i,j)=0P_{c}(i,j)=0 because sjs_{j} has zero code blocks.

Quadratic feature map. A simple weighted sum of per-channel similarities cannot model interactions: it treats simy=0.95\text{sim}_{y}=0.95 and simn=0.60\text{sim}_{n}=0.60 as independent additive contributions, missing the fact that their conjunction provides disproportionately strong evidence of cloning. We therefore lift the similarity profile into a quadratic feature space:

(4) φ⁡(𝐬)=[sy,sn,sc⏟main effects,sy⋅sn,sn⋅sc,sy⋅sc⏟cross-channel interactions]∈ℝ6\varphi(\mathbf{s})=\bigl[\underbrace{s_{y},\;s_{n},\;s_{c}\vphantom{\big|}}_{\text{main effects}},\;\;\underbrace{s_{y}{\cdot}s_{n},\;\;s_{n}{\cdot}s_{c},\;\;s_{y}{\cdot}s_{c}\vphantom{\big|}}_{\text{cross-channel interactions}}\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{6}

where sms_{m} abbreviates simm​(i,j)\text{sim}_{m}(i,j), and any term involving a channel with Pm=0P_{m}=0 is zeroed. The six features decompose into two groups. The main effects capture per-channel evidence: high sns_{n} alone suggests topical similarity. The interaction terms capture cross-channel correspondence: a high sn⋅scs_{n}{\cdot}s_{c} product indicates that both the behavioral specification and the implementation are similar, providing stronger clone evidence than either channel independently. This product-of-similarities formulation replaces the cross-space cosine used in prior multi-modal fusion designs (Liang et al., 2024): computing cos⁡(𝐞in,𝐞jc)\cos(\mathbf{e}^{n}_{i},\mathbf{e}^{c}_{j}) across different LSA subspaces is geometrically ill-defined because the NL and code projections occupy incomparable latent dimensions. The interaction term sn⋅scs_{n}\cdot s_{c} achieves the same goal—capturing NL-Code correspondence—through well-defined within-space similarities.

When Pc=0P_{c}=0, the features scs_{c}, sy⋅scs_{y}{\cdot}s_{c}, and sn⋅scs_{n}{\cdot}s_{c} all vanish, and the model reduces to three active features: [sy,sn,sy⋅sn][s_{y},\;s_{n},\;s_{y}{\cdot}s_{n}]. The learned coefficients for these features absorb the predictive burden, providing principled degradation rather than dilution through a zero-valued channel.

TF-IDF base score. In addition to per-channel similarities, we compute a flat TF-IDF cosine similarity on the full SKILL.md content treated as a single string. This flat score naturally captures cross-channel vocabulary overlap—a skill about IDOR testing will contain “idor” in YAML name, NL body, and code comments simultaneously—providing a strong detection baseline that channel-specific encoding cannot replicate. The flat score is prepended to the feature vector as the first element.

Structural similarity. The structural feature vector 𝐟i\mathbf{f}_{i} (Section 3.3) captures document-level shape. Its similarity simf​(i,j)=1−‖𝐟i−𝐟j‖1/dim(𝐟)\text{sim}_{f}(i,j)=1-\|\mathbf{f}_{i}-\mathbf{f}_{j}\|_{1}/\dim(\mathbf{f}) is appended as the final feature, capturing whether two skills have similar structure (code block count, code fraction, description length) regardless of content.

Logistic fusion. The complete feature vector concatenates the flat TF-IDF score, the quadratic channel features, and structural similarity into an 8-dimensional input:

(5) P⁡(clone∣i,j)=σ⁡(𝐰⊤​[simflat,φ⁡(𝐬),simf]+b)P(\text{clone}\mid i,j)=\sigma\!\bigl(\mathbf{w}^{\top}[\,\text{sim}_{\text{flat}},\;\;\varphi(\mathbf{s}),\;\;\text{sim}_{f}\,]+b\bigr)

where σ⁡(z)=1/(1+e−z)\sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z}) is the logistic sigmoid, and 𝐰∈ℝ8\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^{8}, b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} are learned by maximum likelihood on annotated pairs from SkillClone-Bench with balanced class weights. The 9 parameters (8 weights plus bias) are jointly optimized via MLE with 5-fold stratified cross-validation.

This dual-path design is deliberate. The flat TF-IDF score provides a strong detection baseline—it achieves 0.881 F1 alone (Table 3)—while the channel decomposition adds discriminative evidence that flat text cannot provide: interaction terms model cross-channel correspondence, and the structural feature captures document-shape agreement. The logistic model learns to combine both paths, achieving 0.939 F1 by exploiting their complementarity.

Interpretability. The logistic model retains the per-channel transparency of a weighted sum while adding interaction-level insight. For any flagged pair, the linear combination 𝐰⊤​φ​(𝐬)\mathbf{w}^{\top}\varphi(\mathbf{s}) decomposes into six additive contributions, each corresponding to a named feature. A pair whose dominant contribution is wsn⋅snw_{s_{n}}\cdot s_{n} indicates NL-driven similarity (possible Type-4 semantic clone); a pair dominated by wsy⋅sn⋅sy⋅snw_{s_{y}\cdot s_{n}}\cdot s_{y}\cdot s_{n} indicates metadata-and-instruction alignment without code evidence—the fractal adaptation pattern of Figure 1. This decomposition is valuable for security and governance applications where understanding the nature of a clone relationship matters as much as detecting it.

3.6. Running Example

We illustrate the fusion using the IDOR clone pair from Figure 1. For sis_{i} (zebbern’s original, 26 code blocks) and sjs_{j} (Dokhacgiakhoa’s fractal adaptation, zero code blocks), SkillClone computes: flat TF-IDF similarity =0.61=0.61 (shared IDOR vocabulary across the full documents), channel profile 𝐬=[0.95, 0.60, 0.00]\mathbf{s}=[0.95,\;0.60,\;0.00], and structural similarity =0.38=0.38 (different document shape due to code extraction). Because Pc=0P_{c}=0, the 8-feature vector becomes:

[0.61⏟flat,  0.95,  0.60,  0,0.57⏟sy⋅sn,  0,  0,0.38⏟struct][\,\underbrace{0.61}_{\text{flat}},\;\;0.95,\;\;0.60,\;\;0,\;\;\underbrace{0.57}_{s_{y}\cdot s_{n}},\;\;0,\;\;0,\;\;\underbrace{0.38}_{\text{struct}}\,]

The flat TF-IDF score provides the base detection signal, while the YAML-NL interaction (0.570.57) adds super-additive evidence. The logistic fusion assigns P⁡(clone)=0.82P(\text{clone})=0.82, well above θ=0.50\theta=0.50. The per-channel profile immediately reveals the clone type: high YAML, moderate NL, absent code ⇒\Rightarrow structural adaptation.

For contrast, two Kubernetes skills sharing kubectl vocabulary might have flat TF-IDF =0.55=0.55 but 𝐬=[0.45, 0.55, 0.40]\mathbf{s}=[0.45,\;0.55,\;0.40] with low interactions, yielding P⁡(clone)=0.31P(\text{clone})=0.31—correctly rejected.

3.7. Clone Type Classification

Once the logistic fusion identifies a clone (P⁡(clone)≥θP(\text{clone})\geq\theta), the similarity profile 𝐬=[sy,sn,sc]\mathbf{s}=[s_{y},s_{n},s_{c}] directly determines the clone type. Rather than partitioning the profile space with ad hoc score ranges, we define three Boolean predicates that each encode a structural property from the classical clone taxonomy (Table 1), then compose them into a deterministic decision tree.

Predicates. Let 𝒫\mathcal{P} denote the set of channels present in both skills and 𝐬𝒫\mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{P}} the corresponding sub-vector.

  • •

    Near-Identical(𝐬)(\mathbf{s}): min⁡(𝐬𝒫)≥τ1\;\min(\mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{P}})\geq\tau_{1}. All present channels are near-verbatim—the defining property of Type-1 (“exact except layout/comments”).

  • •

    Uniform(𝐬)(\mathbf{s}): max⁡(𝐬𝒫)−min⁡(𝐬𝒫)≤δ\;\max(\mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{P}})-\min(\mathbf{s}_{\mathcal{P}})\leq\delta. Channel similarities agree within tolerance δ\delta—structure is preserved, consistent with Type-2 (“cosmetic relabeling”).

  • •

    NL-Code-Split(𝐬)(\mathbf{s}): sn≥τ2∧(sc<τ2∨Pc=0)\;s_{n}\geq\tau_{2}\;\wedge\;(s_{c}<\tau_{2}\;\vee\;P_{c}{=}0). The intent channel (NL) shows similarity but the implementation channel (code) diverges or is absent—the defining signature of Type-4 (“same semantics, different syntax”).

Decision tree. The three predicates compose into a four-leaf tree with no overlapping regions:

  1. (1)

    If Near-Identical(𝐬)(\mathbf{s}): Type-1.

  2. (2)

    Else if Uniform(𝐬)(\mathbf{s}): Type-2.

  3. (3)

    Else if NL-Code-Split(𝐬)(\mathbf{s}): Type-4.

  4. (4)

    Else: Type-3 (asymmetric profile with partial channel edits).

The ordering is deliberate: Type-1 is a strict subset of Type-2 (all near-identical profiles are also uniform), so it must be tested first. Type-4 is tested before the Type-3 fallback because the NL-Code split is a specific pattern of asymmetry that warrants its own category.

Parameters. The tree requires only three values: τ1\tau_{1} (identity threshold), δ\delta (uniformity tolerance), and τ2\tau_{2} (semantic threshold), tuned on the validation split. In our evaluation, τ1=0.90\tau_{1}=0.90, δ=0.20\delta=0.20, τ2=0.50\tau_{2}=0.50.

Example. The IDOR pair from Figure 1 has 𝐬=[0.95, 0.60, 0.00]\mathbf{s}=[0.95,\;0.60,\;0.00] with Pc=0P_{c}=0. Near-Identical fails (min=0.60<0.90\min=0.60<0.90). Uniform fails (0.95−0.60=0.35>0.200.95-0.60=0.35>0.20). NL-Code-Split: sn=0.60≥0.50s_{n}=0.60\geq 0.50 and Pc=0P_{c}=0 ⇒\Rightarrow true, so the pair is classified as Type-4. The decision trace is fully auditable: each predicate maps to a named property from the clone taxonomy.

Scalability. At ecosystem scale (NN = 20K, ∼\sim200M candidate pairs), we exploit the dense LSA embeddings for efficient batch cosine similarity via matrix multiplication. An NL-channel pre-filter at θcand=0.10\theta_{\text{cand}}=0.10 reduces candidates by over 90%, enabling full multi-modal scoring in under 30 seconds on a single CPU.

4. Evaluation

We evaluate SkillClone to answer four research questions:

RQ1 (Detection Effectiveness)::

How effective is SkillClone at detecting clone relationships overall and across clone types, compared to single-channel and token-based baselines?

RQ2 (Ablation)::

How does each modality channel and the cross-modal alignment contribute to detection performance?

RQ3 (Ecosystem Analysis)::

What clone patterns does SkillClone reveal at ecosystem scale?

RQ4 (Security Propagation)::

How do known-malicious skill patterns propagate through clone relationships?

4.1. Registry Corpus

We crawled the skillsmp.com registry, retrieving SKILL.md content for 155,547 of 196,134 listed skills (79.3% success rate; failures due to deleted or private repositories). The corpus totals 1.19 GB (avg. 7.6 KB per skill); 78% of skills contain code blocks and 43% are code-heavy (>>50% code), confirming the need for multi-modal analysis.

4.2. Benchmark Construction

No benchmark exists for clone detection on multi-modal agent skills. We construct SkillClone-Bench, a balanced benchmark of 300 ground-truth pairs (150 positive, 150 negative) with stratified difficulty across both classes.

Design principles. We prioritize quality over quantity: each pair is included for a specific evaluation purpose, and both classes are stratified by difficulty so that aggregate metrics are not dominated by trivial cases. Positives span four clone types at increasing difficulty; negatives range from obvious non-matches to deliberately confusing same-category pairs. We avoid manual labeling entirely—all labels derive from verifiable provenance (fork trees) or controlled generation (mutations).

Positive pairs (150). We draw equally from two complementary sources, each contributing 75 pairs:

Fork-mined pairs (75) exploit GitHub fork relationships as verifiable provenance. When a developer forks a skill repository and modifies its contents, the fork tree confirms derivation. We match skills across forks by file path and name similarity, then stratify by modification level into Type-1 (verbatim), Type-2 (renamed), Type-3 (structurally modified), and Type-4 (semantically equivalent but rewritten).

Synthetic mutations (75) ensure coverage of controlled difficulty levels via seven operators applied to randomly sampled seed skills: M1 (identifier renaming, Type-2), M2 (NL paraphrasing with synonym replacement and 30% content removal, Type-3), M3 (code stripping that retains only NL section headers, Type-4), M4 (content extension, Type-3), M5 (content subsetting, Type-3), M6 (cross-skill combination, Type-3), and M7 (full semantic rewrite via LLM paraphrase, Type-4). M3 and M7 produce the hardest pairs: both preserve functional intent while eliminating surface-level token overlap.

Negative pairs (150). To avoid easy-negative inflation, we stratify negatives by difficulty:

Easy negatives (50) pair skills from different categories (e.g., DevOps vs. documentation), providing clear non-clones where low similarity is expected.

Hard negatives (100) pair skills from the same category whose multi-modal similarity falls in [0.15,0.45][0.15,0.45]. These pairs share topical vocabulary (e.g., two Kubernetes skills both referencing kubectl and namespace) without being clones. Hard negatives constitute two-thirds of the negative set, deliberately stressing the detector’s ability to distinguish vocabulary overlap from genuine cloning.

Table 2 summarizes the composition. Within positives, easy pairs (Type-1/2) are near-verbatim copies detectable by any approach, while hard pairs (Type-3/4, 55% of positives) involve structural modifications or semantic rewrites that challenge single-channel detectors. Within negatives, easy pairs cross category boundaries (e.g., DevOps vs. documentation), while hard pairs share the same category and topical vocabulary (e.g., two Kubernetes skills) without being clones. Hard negatives constitute two-thirds of the negative set, deliberately stressing the detector’s false-positive rate. We release SkillClone-Bench as part of our replication package.

4.3. Experimental Setup

Baselines. We compare against four modality-matched approaches:

  • •

    TF-IDF (flat text): Standard TF-IDF cosine similarity on the full SKILL.md content as a single string, ignoring modality structure.

  • •

    MinHash: Locality-sensitive hashing on character nn-grams (n=5n\!=\!5) of the full skill text, representing a scalable token-based baseline.

  • •

    NL-Only: SkillClone’s NL channel embedding applied in isolation, representing the strongest single-channel baseline.

  • •

    Code-Only: SkillClone’s code channel embedding applied in isolation.

Baseline Scope. Our goal is to compare SkillClone against baselines that preserve the task definition, namely clone detection over full multi-modal skill documents rather than over extracted code fragments alone. We therefore do not present this evaluation as an exhaustive state-of-the-art bakeoff against every recent code-clone model. Instead, we compare against strong text and token baselines plus single-channel ablations that operate on the same underlying artifacts. We do not include neural code clone detectors such as SAGA (Wu et al., 2024), DeepSim (Zhao and Huang, 2018), or MAGNET (Zhang and Saber, 2025) because they require single-language parseable source code as input (ASTs, PDGs, or token sequences). Agent skills are not parseable programs, because they interleave YAML frontmatter, natural language prose, and code blocks in multiple languages within a single document. Applying these tools would require discarding the NL and YAML channels (78% of skill content by volume), fundamentally changing the detection task. The NL-Only and Code-Only ablations in Table 3 quantify the cost of this single-channel restriction: both achieve lower F1 than multi-modal fusion.

Metrics. We report precision, recall, and F1 score for binary clone detection. For each approach, we find the optimal threshold via grid search on SkillClone-Bench to ensure a fair comparison at each method’s best operating point. For clone type analysis, we report per-type recall.

Environment. All experiments run on a single machine with 32 GB RAM and an Intel Xeon CPU. We implement SkillClone and baselines in Python, using scikit-learn for TF-IDF and logistic regression. The full evaluation code and data are included in our replication package.

4.4. RQ1: Detection Effectiveness

Table 3 presents the results. SkillClone achieves the highest F1 (0.939) with both the highest precision (0.952) and recall (0.927). It also achieves perfect recall on Type-1–3 and the highest Type-4 recall (81%), outperforming TF-IDF (67%) and MinHash (19%). The interaction terms in the logistic fusion capture cross-channel correspondence that flat bag-of-words cannot model: a pair with high YAML and moderate NL receives a super-additive boost that TF-IDF misses. 5-fold cross-validation estimates SkillClone’s generalization F1 at 0.920 (±\pm0.026).

MinHash achieves high precision (0.962) but sacrifices recall (0.673), missing one-third of clones. The single-channel baselines (NL-Only 0.830, Code-Only 0.732) confirm that combining channels via logistic fusion substantially outperforms any single modality.

Per-Type and Error Analysis. The per-type columns reveal where multi-modal fusion provides the greatest advantage. All approaches achieve ≥\geq94% recall on Type-1–3, but the critical differentiation emerges for Type-4 semantic clones. SkillClone achieves 81% Type-4 recall (46/57), which is 4.2×\times higher than MinHash and 1.2×\times higher than TF-IDF. MinHash fails on Type-4 because these clones share minimal surface tokens; TF-IDF captures some through vocabulary overlap but cannot model cross-channel interactions.

SkillClone produces 11 false negatives and 7 false positives on SkillClone-Bench. All 11 false negatives are Type-4 pairs where both NL and code differ substantially despite shared functional intent, making them the hardest cases at the boundary of what structural similarity can detect. Among false positives, the dominant category is same-category hard negatives where shared domain vocabulary (e.g., two Kubernetes skills with kubectl tokens) inflates similarity across channels.

4.5. RQ2: Ablation Study

Table 4 validates that every component contributes. The largest single-component impact comes from channel decomposition: removing all channel features (“TF-IDF only” row) costs −-6.1pp, confirming that per-channel similarity and interaction terms provide substantial evidence beyond flat document similarity. Structural features contribute −-4.9pp, reflecting the discriminative value of document-level shape (code block count, code fraction) for distinguishing clones from same-category non-clones. The TF-IDF base contributes −-3.2pp, confirming its role as a strong detection signal. The YAML and code channels each contribute approximately −-1pp individually.

4.6. RQ3: Ecosystem-Scale Analysis

We apply SkillClone to 20,247 skills with full content crawled from GitHub and SkillsMP to characterize clone patterns at ecosystem scale.

Table 5 summarizes the ecosystem-level findings. We highlight three observations that challenge common assumptions about agent skill ecosystems.

4.6.1. Finding 1: Most duplication is creative, not lazy

Only 9.7% of skills are exact (SHA-256) duplicates, yet 75% participate in clone relationships. The gap reveals that the dominant form of duplication is modification—developers copy a skill and adapt it rather than reusing it verbatim. Within name-based clone clusters, 96% of skill pairs are modified variants and only 4% are byte-identical copies. The median coefficient of variation in content length within clusters is 0.35, and the mean max/min ratio is 5.5×\times—meaning that skills sharing the same name vary by more than 5×\times in length on average.

The most extreme variation occurs in document-handling skills: the “pdf” family spans 541 to 56,613 characters (104.6×\times range), “web-search” spans 212 to 22,569 characters (106.5×\times), and “setup” spans 541 to 76,278 characters (141×\times). These ranges reflect a spectrum from minimal stubs to comprehensive implementations of the same concept. This contrasts sharply with traditional package ecosystems where reuse is mediated by dependency declarations and verbatim copies are rare (Zimmermann et al., 2019). In the skill ecosystem, the copy-and-modify workflow is the primary reuse mechanism, and it is entirely invisible to the registry infrastructure.

4.6.2. Finding 2: Extreme author concentration and mirroring

The top 10 authors (0.9% of 1,060 total) produce 57.8% of all skills, with a Gini coefficient of 0.868—more concentrated than income inequality in most OECD countries. This is far more extreme than npm, where the top 1% of maintainers account for ∼\sim10% of packages (Zimmermann et al., 2019).

Clone analysis reveals two distinct author archetypes. Originators create novel skills that are subsequently copied by others: davila7 (663 skills, 49% shared with other authors) and openclaw (3,423 skills, 11% shared) are prolific creators whose work propagates through the ecosystem. Aggregators collect and rebrand others’ work: clawdbot (283 skills, 99% shared) is the most extreme case—its clawdbot/skills repository contains 236 skills of which 234 are byte-for-byte identical to openclaw/skills, a wholesale mirroring operation invisible to registry users. A third archetype, independent creators (a5c-ai, GPTomics, rmyndharis: 0% shared), produces entirely original content with no detected clones in the ecosystem. The interplay between these archetypes drives ecosystem growth: originators create templates, aggregators amplify them, and independent creators add genuinely novel capabilities.

4.6.3. Finding 3: Clone lineages show a long tail of improvement

To understand whether copying produces value, we trace popular skill families chronologically using GitHub repository creation dates and content metrics. We examine six families with ≥\geq20 copies each.

In the pdf family (24 copies, 21 authors, 18 unique versions), phodal published a minimal 541-character stub, while invariantlabs-ai created a 7K-character template (April 2025) copied verbatim by 5+ authors (byte-identical at 7,068 characters). However, jjyaoao expanded the skill to 56,613 characters (8×\times the template) with 46 code blocks covering advanced PDF operations, and openclaw reorganized it into 9.9K characters with 49 code blocks. The skill-creator family (62 copies, 52 authors) shows a similar 27.5×\times range from a 1.7K-character skeleton to a 48K-character comprehensive guide with 28 code blocks. The code-review family (34 copies, 30 authors) exhibits a structural shift: later versions are 1.4×\times longer but contain 60% fewer code blocks, reflecting a trend toward NL-heavy behavioral specifications rather than code-heavy scripts.

These patterns suggest that the ecosystem’s copy-and-modify workflow, while producing many zero-value verbatim copies, also enables a long tail of genuine improvement.

Partial clones and superseded skills. To quantify this, we classify clone relationships within each family. Of 9,460 clone pairs in families with ≤\leq15 members, 46% are extensions (the longer version contains >>70% of the shorter version’s key content plus additional material) and 54% are divergent (partial overlap with different structural choices). The extension pattern dominates in document-handling families: the “pdf” family’s 7K template reappears in the 57K extended version with all original sections preserved and 29 new code blocks added. This confirms that partial cloning in the skill ecosystem functions as progressive enhancement, not just copying.

We further identify 483 skills that are strict subsets of another skill in the same family (>>70% of their key content lines appear verbatim in a longer variant). More broadly, ranking skills within each family by a quality composite (content length, NL coverage, code block count), we find that 41% of skills in clone families (2,360 of 5,735) are superseded—a strictly better variant exists. In the “pdf” family, 25 of 26 copies are superseded by jjyaoao’s comprehensive version; in “skill-creator,” 59 of 62 are superseded. This means that a user browsing the registry has a 41% chance of discovering an inferior version when a better one exists under a different author. Clone detection enables quality-aware deduplication: rather than removing duplicates, a registry could surface the best variant in each cluster and link related alternatives.

Cross-category migration. We additionally observe that the same skill concept appears under different registry categories depending on who publishes it. The “pptx” family spans four categories (DevOps, content-media, skill-tools, documentation); “development” spans seven. This inconsistency suggests that the current category taxonomy is unreliable as an organization mechanism, and that clone-based clustering could provide a more principled skill ontology.

After deduplication, the 20K registry collapses to 5,642 unique skill concepts (3.5×\times inflation). Nearly half (4,468) are true singletons; the rest form 1,174 clusters.

4.7. RQ4: Security Propagation

Rather than assembling synthetic proof-of-concepts, we scan the 20K corpus for real security-relevant skills using regex patterns for six categories of dangerous code: SQL injection payloads, XSS test vectors, reverse shell commands, command injection via unsafe subprocess calls, hardcoded secrets, and unsafe eval on user input. We then use SkillClone to trace how these confirmed patterns propagate through clone relationships.

Table 6 shows the results. We identify 141 seed skills containing real security-relevant code, of which 127 (90%) have at least one clone in the ecosystem. These 141 seeds link to 1,100 total clones maintained by 119 distinct authors. Critically, 777 clones (71%) cross author boundaries, meaning the security pattern propagated to developers who did not write the original code.

Pattern propagation. Of the 1,100 clones, 316 (29%) inherited the security-relevant code pattern itself—not just similar content, but the actual dangerous code. The remaining 71% are structural or semantic clones where the security pattern was modified or removed during adaptation. The most prolific propagator is the “pentest-commands” family: davila7’s 22K-star pentesting skill (containing SQL injection and XSS payloads) has 30 clones across 22 different authors, of which 9 preserved the original exploit code. davila7’s “Linux Privilege Escalation” skill (containing reverse shell commands) propagated to 15 clones across 12 authors.

Implications. A registry maintainer who flags and removes one pentesting skill would miss 30 clones carrying the same exploit code under different names and authors. Without clone-based propagation analysis, the true blast radius of a single security-relevant skill remains hidden.

5. Discussion

5.1. Clone Detection vs. Reuse Inference

Clone detection establishes structural similarity, not derivation. Reuse inference asks whether sjs_{j} was causally derived from sis_{i} and therefore requires additional provenance signals such as fork relationships, commit timestamps, or explicit attribution.

In some cases, clone detection directly enables reuse confirmation. The LabArchives example (Figure 1) is unambiguous: 99.7% character similarity on 260 lines of niche scientific content, combined with the added skill-author: K-Dense Inc. metadata, constitutes a smoking gun. Our fork-mined benchmark pairs similarly provide ground-truth reuse via GitHub provenance. For the broader ecosystem analysis (RQ3), however, we report clone prevalence, not reuse prevalence: the 258K detected pairs include both intentional copies and cases of convergent development where different authors independently produced similar skills.

For security applications (RQ4), the clone-vs-reuse distinction is immaterial. Whether two skills share a vulnerability through copying or convergent development, the blast radius is identical. Clone detection is sufficient to identify the set of skills that share a malicious pattern, regardless of how they came to share it.

5.2. Implications

Our findings carry implications for multiple stakeholders. For skill registry operators, the 75% clone involvement rate and 41% superseded-skill rate suggest that deduplication and provenance tracking should be first-class ecosystem features. For security teams, 90% of security-relevant seed skills have at least one clone, yielding 1,100 downstream clones (777 cross-author), so per-skill vulnerability scanning is insufficient and clone-based propagation analysis is necessary to identify the full blast radius.

Precision and Recall Tradeoff. On SkillClone-Bench, flat-text TF-IDF is a strong baseline, achieving 0.897 precision, 0.867 recall, and 0.881 F1. However, SkillClone improves on all three metrics, reaching 0.952 precision, 0.927 recall, and 0.939 F1 by combining flat similarity with per-channel evidence. This difference matters more at ecosystem scale than on SkillClone-Bench alone: in a 20K-skill corpus, small precision gaps translate into many spurious clone edges. Additionally, flat-text TF-IDF cannot distinguish clone types, while SkillClone preserves the per-channel signal needed to separate exact copies from harder semantic clones.

5.3. Limitations

Our current study prioritizes task-faithful multi-modal analysis over exhaustive model coverage. The evaluation therefore focuses on modality-matched baselines rather than every recent neural code-clone detector, many of which assume single-language source code input. In addition, although our crawl retrieved 155K skill files, the clone-graph analysis reported here uses 20K skills and a 300-pair benchmark. Larger annotated datasets and full-corpus runs would improve confidence in the reported clone-type distribution and propagation estimates. Our three-channel decomposition is also intentionally scoped to the primary in-file modalities of SKILL.md artifacts, excluding auxiliary repository context such as linked files, screenshots, and commit history.

5.4. Threats to Validity

Internal validity. The benchmark relies partly on synthetic mutations; we mitigate this with fork-mined pairs and manual labels. Fusion weights are optimized on SkillClone-Bench and may not generalize; the ablation shows robustness to component removal.

External validity. Our 20K-skill sample is substantial but may not represent the full 196K ecosystem. The observed 75% clone-involvement rate and 3.5×\times inflation ratio may shift under a larger or more complete crawl.

Construct validity. The clone type taxonomy adapted from source code may not capture all multi-modal similarity patterns. Threshold-based type boundaries are heuristic; a learned classifier may improve accuracy. The inter-annotator agreement (κ=0.81\kappa=0.81) is substantial but not perfect. Our ecosystem analysis reports clone prevalence, not confirmed reuse; the Type-4 dominance may include convergent development cases that are structurally similar but causally independent.

6. Related Work

6.1. Code Clone Detection

Code clone detection has been studied extensively over two decades (Roy et al., 2009). Representative classical approaches include token-based systems such as CCFinder and CP-Miner (Kamiya et al., 2002; Li et al., 2006), tree-based systems such as NiCad and Deckard (Roy and Cordy, 2008; Jiang et al., 2007), and scalable index-based systems such as SourcererCC (Sajnani et al., 2016). BigCloneBench (Svajlenko et al., 2014) standardized evaluation, while newer neural approaches such as DeepSim, CCLearner, SAGA, and MAGNET target harder semantic clones (Zhao and Huang, 2018; Li et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2024; Zhang and Saber, 2025). However, these methods assume source code as the primary artifact. SkillClone instead targets multi-modal skill documents that interleave natural language, YAML metadata, and embedded code, extending clone detection to a new class of software artifacts.

6.2. Software Ecosystem Analysis

Large-scale ecosystem studies have characterized dependency structure and systemic risk in registries such as npm and PyPI (Zimmermann et al., 2019; Wittern et al., 2016; Kikas et al., 2017; Decan et al., 2019; Bommarito and Bommarito, 2019). Recent work has also begun to characterize the architecture and growth of agent-skill ecosystems (Xu and Yan, 2026; Ling et al., 2026). However, prior studies do not model inter-skill clone relationships. This omission is particularly important in a flat ecosystem with no dependency mechanism, where reuse is implicit rather than declared. SkillClone addresses this gap by inferring clone relationships directly from content similarity and constructing the first clone graph for agent skills.

6.3. Supply Chain Security

Software supply chain research has shown that vulnerabilities and malicious packages propagate through ecosystem structure rather than through isolated artifacts alone (Liu et al., 2022; Ohm et al., 2020; Duan et al., 2021). In agent ecosystems, recent tools focus on per-skill analysis for vulnerability detection, formal verification, malicious tool identification, prompt injection, and MCP-server risks (Liu et al., 2026b; Bhardwaj, 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Zhao et al., 2025; Hasan et al., 2025; Jia et al., 2026; Schmotz et al., 2026; Schmotz et al., 2025; Maloyan and Namiot, 2026). The January 2026 ClawHavoc campaign (Koi Security, 2026) underscores the practical importance of these risks. SkillClone complements this line of work by adding clone-graph analysis: instead of inspecting each skill in isolation, it traces reuse links to estimate the blast radius of malicious or vulnerable patterns.

7. Conclusion

We presented SkillClone, the first multi-modal clone detection approach for agent skills, fusing YAML, NL, and code similarity with cross-modal alignment. On SkillClone-Bench (300 pairs), SkillClone achieves F1 of 0.939, outperforming TF-IDF (0.881) and achieving 4.2×\times higher Type-4 recall than MinHash. Applied to 20K skills, SkillClone reveals 258K clone pairs involving 75% of all skills, with 40% cross-author reuse and a 3.5×\times ecosystem inflation ratio after deduplication. Security propagation analysis identifies 141 real security-relevant seed skills whose patterns reach 1,100 clones across 119 affected authors. We distinguish clone detection from reuse inference, showing clone analysis is both independently valuable for security and enables downstream reuse discovery when combined with provenance signals.

Data Availability

Our replication package, including SkillClone-Bench, the SkillClone implementation, and all evaluation scripts, will be made publicly available upon publication.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
